lead: Set a few reliable rules of thumb for small things, so you don't have to think everything through from scratch every time.
when: When you face too many small decisions, keep going back and forth, or already have some dependable experience to draw on, give it a try.
body:
Glancing at the sky before you head out in the morning, restarting your phone when it acts up, checking the return policy before you buy something: these are all heuristics. The word sounds technical, but the idea is simple: use a handy rule of thumb to help you decide a bit faster. It usually isn't the perfect method, but the time and energy it saves are worth something too.

In cognitive psychology, a heuristic is a rule of thumb or mental shortcut people use to simplify judgments and solve problems. It lowers the cost of thinking but doesn't guarantee the best answer.

Why do we need them? Because there are simply too many things to decide in a day. What to have for lunch or when to reply to a message isn't worth a full analysis every time. Still, experience has a "shelf life" and a limited range: a rule that works well most of the time needs to be swapped out when something unusual comes up.
example:
Whenever you're waiting on a reply, you agonize: "Should I nudge them? Will I seem pushy?" Eventually you set a rule for ordinary work emails: if there's no reply after three business days, follow up once, politely, and spell out what you need next.

Now you no longer fret about it every day. But if the other person is handling the venue for tomorrow's event, you can't just wait three days; you agree on a time to confirm in advance. A good rule lets you worry less and still leaves a way out for emergencies.
extra: A beginner cook adds salt exactly as the recipe says. With practice, they add a little less first, taste, and then add more. "Start with less, add more later" is a handy rule of thumb: it won't make every dish perfect, but it's much easier to fix than pouring in too much at once.
steps: Pick a small thing you keep agonizing over and set a simple rule for it.
Write down the exceptions too: when shouldn't you follow it, and when do you need to think of something else?
Try it for a week or two and see whether it actually saves you energy or creates more hassle.
caution: Catchy rules of thumb aren't always reliable. "Expensive means good" and "If everyone's buying it, it can't be wrong" are shortcuts too, and they can cost you. For high-stakes decisions like buying a home or signing an important contract, don't rely on a one-liner alone.
exercise: Find a small thing you've already agonized over three times this week and write one sentence: "Next time this happens, I'll first..." Then add: "But if..., I won't follow it."
brief: A map of a shortcut versus a full search: a stick figure looks for fruit among many trees and follows a short trail of footprints to quickly find a basket of fruit; beside it, a longer thin gray search route visits more trees and might find bigger fruit.
